title: Digestion
in30Seconds: Digestion is the process of breaking food into smaller pieces the body can use. The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases describes it as breaking nutrients into parts small enough for the body to absorb and use for energy, growth, and cell repair. The work happens along the digestive tract — the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine — using two kinds of breakdown: mechanical, like chewing and churning, and chemical, like enzymes and acids.
whyItMatters: Every bite of food is useless to the body until digestion frees the nutrients inside it. A sandwich's bread, cheese, and lettuce cannot be used as they are; they must be taken apart first. Understanding digestion explains why we chew, why a meal takes hours to process, and why the stomach is not the only player in the game. It also sets up the next step in nutrition science: once food is broken down, the body absorbs those nutrients — a process covered in its own lesson. Digestion is where nutrition stops being about food and becomes about the body.
learningObjectives: Define digestion as the process of breaking food into pieces small enough for the body to absorb and use.
Name the organs of the digestive tract — mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine — and state the main job of each.
Distinguish mechanical breakdown (chewing, churning, and mixing) from chemical breakdown (enzymes and acids).
Trace the path of a bite of food from the mouth to the point where nutrients are ready for the body.
Explain that absorbed nutrients enter the body through the bloodstream and that absorption is a separate topic from digestion.

collegeVersion.heading: What digestion is
collegeVersion.body: Digestion is the process of breaking food into smaller and smaller pieces until the nutrients inside are small enough for the body to use. The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) puts it directly: the digestive system breaks nutrients into parts small enough for the body to absorb and use for energy, growth, and cell repair. That working definition matters because it sets the bar for the whole process. A slice of bread is not useful to the body as a slice of bread; the starch inside it must be reduced to simple sugars, the protein to amino acids, and so on. Nothing in the body can use food in its original form, so digestion is not an optional courtesy but a required first step. It is also worth noting that digestion is not one single event. It is a series of steps spread across several organs, each doing a different kind of work, and it takes hours from first bite to finished nutrients.

collegeVersion.heading: The digestive tract, organ by organ
collegeVersion.body: The digestive tract is a long, twisting tube that runs from the mouth to the anus. Its main organs are the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine. Each has a clear job. The mouth starts the work: teeth cut and grind food into smaller pieces while saliva moistens it and begins chemically breaking down starches. The esophagus is the delivery chute: wave-like muscle contractions called peristalsis push the swallowed food down to the stomach. The stomach is the mixing tank: its muscles churn the food while glands in its lining release stomach acid and digestive enzymes, producing a soupy mixture that slowly empties into the small intestine. The small intestine is where most of the chemical work gets finished: it mixes the food with digestive juices from the pancreas and liver, completing the breakdown of proteins, carbohydrates, and fats, and it absorbs most of the nutrients. The large intestine is the finishing line: it absorbs water and turns the remaining waste into stool. Each organ hands off to the next, and the whole trip is powered by peristalsis.

collegeVersion.heading: Mechanical versus chemical breakdown
collegeVersion.body: The body breaks food down in two different ways, and it uses both at once. Mechanical breakdown is physical: chewing with the teeth, churning in the stomach, and squeezing and mixing along the tract. It makes pieces smaller without changing what they are made of; a chewed carrot is still carrot, just in smaller bits. Chemical breakdown changes the food itself: enzymes and acids split large molecules into smaller ones. Saliva carries an enzyme that begins breaking starches into sugars in the mouth. Stomach acid and the stomach's enzymes attack proteins. The pancreas sends enzymes that work on carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, and the liver's bile helps break down fats. None of these chemical tools is visible, which is why the chemical side of digestion is easy to forget, but without it the mechanical side would only produce smaller lumps of food, not nutrients. The two work as a team: mechanical breakdown exposes more surface area so the chemical tools can reach more of the food.

collegeVersion.heading: From bite to nutrients, and what happens next
collegeVersion.body: Tracing one bite shows how the steps connect. A bite of oatmeal with milk enters the mouth, where teeth grind it and saliva starts on the starches. Swallowing sends it down the esophagus to the stomach, where acid and enzymes attack the proteins and the churning turns it into a soupy mix. That mix moves into the small intestine, where pancreatic enzymes, bile, and the intestine's own juices finish the breakdown: starches become simple sugars, proteins become amino acids, and fats become fatty acids and glycerol. By the time the contents reach the large intestine, the useful parts have been released and mostly absorbed; the large intestine reclaims water, and what remains becomes stool. The nutrients that were freed do not stay in the tract. They cross into the bloodstream and are carried to the rest of the body — that crossing is absorption, a process covered in its own lesson. The breakdown itself, though, is digestion's job, and it is the reason the body can get anything at all out of a meal. Digestion is best understood as a demolition crew with a recycling plant attached: it takes structures apart so the useful materials can be hauled away and reused.

vocabulary.definition: The process of breaking food into smaller pieces, down to nutrients small enough for the body to absorb and use for energy, growth, and cell repair.
The long, twisting tube of hollow organs from the mouth to the anus through which food travels and is broken down.
The physical reduction of food into smaller pieces through actions such as chewing, squeezing, and churning.
The splitting of food molecules into smaller molecules using digestive juices such as enzymes, stomach acid, and bile.
A chemical tool made by the body that splits food molecules apart, such as the saliva enzyme that begins breaking down starches.
A chemical tool such as stomach acid that helps break food down, especially proteins, in the stomach.
Wave-like muscle contractions that push food and liquid along the esophagus and through the rest of the digestive tract.
A substance in food, such as protein, carbohydrate, fat, vitamin, mineral, or water, that the body uses for energy, growth, and cell repair.
The soupy mixture of food and digestive juices that the stomach releases into the small intestine.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Digestion is what your body does to a bite of food before the food can do anything for you. Think of a whole apple: your body cannot use an apple as an apple. It has to be taken apart, first into smaller chunks, then into even smaller pieces, until what is left is the nutrients inside. That taking-apart work is digestion. It happens along a long tube called the digestive tract, from your mouth to your large intestine, and it uses two kinds of tools: your teeth and stomach muscles for the smashing, and your enzymes and acids for the dissolving.
eli10.analogy: Digestion is like a demolition crew working inside an old building. The crew first swings sledgehammers to knock walls into chunks, then uses chemical torches and solvents to break the chunks into raw materials like bricks and metal that can be reused.
eli10.analogyLimits: The demolition crew analogy ends where recycling begins: in real digestion, the broken-down nutrients are absorbed into the body, which is the next step, absorption, and not part of this lesson. A real demolition also throws a lot away, while the body's crew keeps almost everything useful.

workedExample: Picture a breakfast of oatmeal with banana slices and a glass of milk. The first breakdown is mechanical: teeth crush and grind the oats and banana while the tongue mixes them with saliva, which is already chemically working on the starches. Swallowing hands the mash to the esophagus, where wave-like contractions push it to the stomach. The stomach churns the mixture while acid and enzymes attack the proteins in the milk. Hours later, the soupy contents enter the small intestine, where enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver finish the job: the oatmeal's starch becomes simple sugars, the milk's protein becomes amino acids, and its fat becomes fatty acids and glycerol. By the end of the tract, the food you ate no longer exists as food — only nutrients and waste remain, and the nutrients are ready to enter the body.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking digestion happens only in the stomach.
commonMistakes.correction: Breakdown starts in the mouth with chewing and saliva, continues in the stomach, and is mostly finished in the small intestine, which does the bulk of the chemical work.
Digestion breaks food down into smaller pieces; absorption is the separate step in which those pieces cross into the body. Absorption gets its own lesson.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing that swallowing is what moves food down the esophagus.
commonMistakes.correction: Swallowing starts the trip, but wave-like muscle contractions called peristalsis do the pushing, which is why food still reaches the stomach even if you lean back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming chemical breakdown means only stomach acid.
commonMistakes.correction: Chemical tools include saliva enzymes in the mouth, stomach acid and enzymes in the stomach, and pancreatic enzymes plus bile in the small intestine.

compareContrast.label: Mechanical vs. Chemical breakdown
compareContrast.first: Mechanical breakdown is physical: teeth, churning, and mixing make food pieces smaller without changing what they are made of.
compareContrast.second: Chemical breakdown uses enzymes, acids, and bile to split food molecules into smaller molecules, changing the food itself.

compareContrast.label: Digestion vs. Absorption
compareContrast.first: Digestion breaks food down into nutrients small enough for the body to use; it happens inside the digestive tract.
compareContrast.second: Absorption moves those nutrients out of the tract and into the bloodstream; it is covered in its own lesson.

keyTakeaway: Digestion is the body's demolition crew with a recycling plant attached: it breaks every bite into nutrients small enough for the body to use, and the moment those nutrients cross into the body, the separate process of absorption begins.

questionBank.prompt: A slice of toast enters the body and is eventually broken down until the nutrients inside it are small enough to be used. Which term names that whole taking-apart process?
options: Absorption
Digestion
Peristalsis
Hydration
questionBank.explanation: Digestion is the process of breaking food into smaller pieces, down to nutrients small enough for the body to absorb and use. Absorption is the later step of nutrients crossing into the body, and peristalsis is the muscle motion that moves food along.
questionBank.skill: Defining digestion as the breakdown of food into usable pieces

questionBank.prompt: Nadia swallows a bite of rice and it travels to her stomach. What actually moves the bite along her esophagus?
options: Wave-like muscle contractions called peristalsis
Gravity pulling it straight down
The stomach reaching up to collect it
Air pressure from a deep breath
questionBank.explanation: Peristalsis, the wave-like contractions of the tract's muscle layers, pushes food and liquid through the esophagus and the rest of the GI tract. Gravity is not the driver, and the stomach does not reach upward to grab food.
questionBank.skill: Applying peristalsis to food movement through the esophagus

questionBank.prompt: Devon chews a carrot into smaller pieces while his saliva begins chemically breaking down the carrot's starches. Which statement correctly pairs each action with its type of breakdown?
options: Chewing is chemical; saliva's enzyme work is mechanical
Both actions are mechanical because both happen in the mouth
Chewing is mechanical; saliva's enzyme work is chemical
Both actions are chemical because both change the food's molecules
questionBank.explanation: Chewing is mechanical breakdown, physical size reduction by the teeth. The enzyme in saliva is chemical breakdown, because enzymes split starch molecules into smaller molecules rather than just making pieces smaller.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing mechanical from chemical breakdown in the mouth

questionBank.prompt: After a meal, most of the chemical breakdown of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins is completed in which organ, where food mixes with juices from the pancreas and liver?
options: The esophagus
The stomach
The large intestine
The small intestine
questionBank.explanation: The small intestine mixes food with digestive juice from the pancreas, bile from the liver, and its own juice, completing the breakdown of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. The stomach works earlier in the process, and the large intestine mainly absorbs water.
questionBank.skill: Naming the small intestine as the main site of completed chemical breakdown

questionBank.prompt: A nutrition app tells Lena that the protein in her yogurt will be 'unlocked' as it moves through her body. Which sequence correctly describes where that unlocking happens?
options: Stomach acid and enzymes start attacking the protein, and the small intestine finishes the job with pancreatic enzymes
The esophagus dissolves the protein completely before it reaches the stomach
The large intestine breaks the protein down into amino acids after absorbing water
The mouth's saliva breaks the protein into amino acids during chewing
questionBank.explanation: Stomach acid and enzymes begin breaking down proteins in the stomach, and the small intestine completes the job using pancreatic enzymes, breaking proteins into amino acids. Saliva works on starches, the esophagus only moves food, and the large intestine handles water and waste.
questionBank.skill: Tracing protein breakdown across the stomach and small intestine
